# Colored Bits of Inline Code Go Flat Inside Table Cells

## What happens now

Rich can color the short pieces of code you write between back ticks inside a
markdown document, once you switch that coloring on when you create the
markdown. It works fine in ordinary sentences and in headings: a word like
print comes out in one color, quoted text in another, and the whole thing sits
on a light background so it clearly reads as code.

It does not work the same way inside a table cell. The very same piece of code
in a table row comes back with exactly one flat color. Every word, every
number and every quoted piece looks the same as every other piece, and the
plain code background wins over everything else. The usual colors for code are
simply gone, only in tables.

## What should happen

A piece of code inside a table cell should look the same as that same piece
inside a sentence. The colors picked for keywords, words and quoted text should
survive the trip into the table, so a table full of code snippets is just as
easy to read as the paragraph above it. Tables with plain words keep looking
exactly as they do today.

## About this project

Rich is a Python library for writing nice looking things in the terminal:
colors, tables, progress bars, logs and syntax colored source. It also draws
markdown for you, which is how the command rich-markdown turns a notes file
into something readable in a terminal window. Markdown documents hold both
tables and little snippets of code, and Rich is meant to show them side by
side, in color.

## Problem this solves

People write notes, cheat sheets and command references where the important
part lives inside a table cell. When those cells lose their colors, the table
turns into a wall of one tone and the eye can no longer pick out the words that
matter, which is exactly the job you bought a colored terminal writer for.

## What changed

Colored short pieces of code keep their colors when they land inside a table
cell, in both the heading row and the body rows. Colors stop being flattened
anywhere in a markdown table. Nothing else about tables changes: plain words,
links, bold, italics, headings, code blocks and whole-document colors look the
same as before, and the rich-markdown command keeps taking the same choices it
takes today.

## Impact

Ease of use and correctness of what you see. The colors you asked for now
arrive in tables the same way they arrive in sentences. No setting is added and
none is taken away, so documents and tables written today keep working.

## User experience

Here is a small example of the difference.

Before: I put the word for a print call, written between back ticks, in a cell
of a table in my notes, and I show the file in the terminal. The cell shows
that word in a single dull color, with a gray block behind it, while the same
word in the sentence above the table shows up in several colors. The table
looks broken next to the sentence.

After: I do the same thing and the cell shows that word with the same several
colors as the sentence, so my notes read evenly top to bottom and the code
words in the table stand out just as much as everywhere else.

## Hints

- rich/markdown.py
- tests/test_markdown.py
- rich/text.py
- rich/syntax.py
- docs/source/markdown.rst

- Fixed solo ZWJ crash https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3953
- Fixed control codes reporting width of 1 https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3953

### Fixed

- Fixed characters out of unicode range reporting a cell size if 0 https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3944

## [14.3.0] - 2026-01-24

### Fixed

- IPython now respects when a `Console` instance is passed to `pretty.install` https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3915

- Fixed extra padding on first cell in columns https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3935

- Fixed style new-lines when soft_wrap = True and a print style is set https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3938

### Added

- Added support for some multi-codepopint glyphs (will fix alignment issues for these characters) https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3930
- Added support for `UNICODE_VERSION` environment variable https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3930
- Added `last_render_height` property to LiveRender https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3934
- Expose locals_max_depth and locals_overflow in traceback.install https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3906/
- Added `Segment.split_lines_terminator` https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3938

- `cells.cell_len` now has a `unicode_version` parameter (that you probably should never change) https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3930
- Live will not write a new line if there was nothing rendered https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3934
- Changed style of Markdown headers https://github.com/Textualize/rich/pull/3942
- Changed style of Markdown tables, added `markdown.table.header` and `markdown.ta

Done. Here's what I found and changed.

## Root cause
`TableDataElement.on_text` (used for both `td_open` **and** `th_open`, so header + body cells) did:

```python
text = Text(text) if isinstance(text, str) else text
text.stylize(context.current_style)     # appends a full-length span *after* the token spans
self.content.append_text(text)
```

Inline code reaches this path as a `Text` whose syntax colours are already per-token spans. `Text.render` combines overlapping spans by span-list index, so the trailing whole-cell `markdown.code` span (`bold cyan on black`) overrode every pygments span — one flat colour, code background winning. Plain sentences go through `TextElement.on_text`, which only styles raw strings, so they were never flattened.

## Fix — `rich/markdown.py`
```python
     def on_text(self, context: MarkdownContext, text: TextType) -> None:
-        text = Text(text) if isinstance(text, str) else text
-        text.stylize(context.current_style)
-        self.content.append_text(text)
+        if isinstance(text, str):
+            self.content.append(text, context.current_style)
+        else:
+            self.content.append_text(text)
```
Strings still get the ambient style; pre-styled `Text` (highlighted code, links, etc.) is appended as-is so its spans survive underneath. `Text` import is still used elsewhere in the module. Also added the matching `CHANGELOG.md` entry. No new deps, no public API/CLI change, docs unchanged (upstream docs are byte-identical here).

Verification (real output): `| Doc | ... | print | \`print('hi')\` |` now emits the same `38;2;248;248;242/230;219;116 on 48;2;39;40;34` token sequence in the cell as in the sentence; plain-word tables render byte-identically to before.

## Environment caveat — please read
`tests/test_markdown.py::test_inline_code_in_table_cells` **could not pass** in this container even with the exact upstream fix, and neither could 7 other tests that were already failing before I touched anything (`test_card_render`, 6 `test_syntax` cases). Cause: installed Pygments **2.21.0** changed monokai `Name.Builtin` from `#f8f8f2` to `#a6e22e`, while the repo's `poetry.lock` pins **pygments 2.19.2** (all locked expectations were generated against that). `tests/test_pretty.py` likewise aborted collection on `import attr` although `attrs 21.4.0` is a locked dev dependency.

So the environment did not match the committed lockfile. I aligned it to the lock rather than editing anything else: `pip install pygments==2.19.2 attrs==21.4.0`. I did not touch tests, manifests, or theme code (forcing the old colour in `rich/syntax.py` would have corrupted real syntax highlighting).

## Results (`make test` equivalent, `TERM=unknown pytest tests/ -q`)
- Before, pristine HEAD: `7 failed, 898 passed, 23 skipped` + collection error in `test_pretty.py`
- After fix, old env: `8 failed, 898 passed, 23 skipped` (only markdown item was mine)
- After fix + lockfile alignment: **`956 passed, 24 skipped`** (0 failures); `tests/test_markdown.py tests/test_table.py tests/test_text.py` → `141 passed`

1 │ # Colored Bits of Inline Code Go Flat Inside Table Cells
   2 │ 
   3 │ ## What happens now
   4 │ 
   5 │ Rich can color the short pieces of code you write between back ticks inside a
   6 │ markdown document, once you switch that coloring on when you create the
   7 │ markdown. It works fine in ordinary sentences and in headings: a word like
   8 │ print comes out in one color, quoted text in another, and the whole thing sits
   9 │ on a light background so it clearly reads as code.
  10 │ 
  11 │ It does not work the same way inside a table cell. The very same piece of code
  12 │ in a table row comes back with exactly one flat color. Every word, every
  13 │ number and every quoted piece looks the same as every other piece, and the
  14 │ plain code background wins over everything else. The usual colors for code are
  15 │ simply gone, only in tables.
  16 │ 
  17 │ ## What should happen
  18 │ 
  19 │ A piece of code inside a table cell should look the same as that same piece
  20 │ inside a sentence. The colors picked for keywords, words and quoted text should
  21 │ survive the trip into the table, so a table full of code snippets is just as
  22 │ easy to read as the paragraph above it. Tables with plain words keep looking
  23 │ exactly as they do today.
  24 │ 
  25 │ ## About this project
  26 │ 
  27 │ Rich is a Python library for writing nice looking things in the terminal:
  28 │ colors, tables, progress bars, logs and syntax colored source. It also draws
  29 │ markdown for you, which is how the command rich-markdown turns a notes file
  30 │ into something readable in a terminal window. Markdown documents hold both
  31 │ tables and little snippets of code, and Rich is meant to show them side by
  32 │ side, in color.
  33 │ 
  34 │ ## Problem this solves
  35 │ 
  36 │ People write notes, cheat sheets and command references where the important
  37 │ part lives inside a table cell. When those cells lose their colors, the table
  38 │ turns into a wall of one tone and the eye can no longer pick out the words that
  39 │ matter, which is exactly the job you bought a colored terminal writer for.
  40 │ 
  41 │ ## What changed
  42 │ 
  43 │ Colored short pieces of code keep their colors when they land inside a table
  44 │ cell, in both the heading row and the body rows. Colors stop being flattened
  45 │ anywhere in a markdown table. Nothing else about tables changes: plain words,
  46 │ links, bold, italics, headings, code blocks and whole-document colors look the
  47 │ same as before, and the rich-markdown command keeps taking the same choices it
  48 │ takes today.
  49 │ 
  50 │ ## Impact
  51 │ 
  52 │ Ease of use and correctness of what you see. The colors you asked for now
  53 │ arrive in tables the same way they arrive in sentences. No setting is added and
  54 │ none is taken away, so documents and tables written today keep working.
  55 │ 
  56 │ ## User experience
  57 │ 
  58 │ Here is a small example of the difference.
  59 │ 
  60 │ Before: I put the word for a print call, written between back ticks, in a cell
  61 │ of a table in my notes, and I show the file in the terminal. The cell shows
  62 │ that word in a single dull color, with a gray block behind it, while the same
  63 │ word in the sentence above the table shows up in several colors. The table
  64 │ looks broken next to the sentence.
  65 │ 
  66 │ After: I do the same thing and the cell shows that word with the same several
  67 │ colors as the sentence, so my notes read evenly top to bottom and the code
  68 │ words in the table stand out just as much as everywhere else.
  69 │ 
  70 │ ## Hints
  71 │ 
  72 │ - rich/markdown.py
  73 │ - tests/test_markdown.py
  74 │ - rich/text.py
  75 │ - rich/syntax.py
  76 │ - docs/source/markdown.rst
  77 │

{"content": "# coding=utf-8
"""Regression tests for syntax highlighted inline code inside Markdown tables.

The tests here cover https://github.com/Textualize/rich/issues/4038, where a
snippet in back ticks was rendered in a single flat color inside a table cell,
while the very same snippet in a paragraph kept the colors of the code theme.

"""

import io
import re

from rich.console import Console, RenderableType
from rich.markdown import Markdown

SNIPPET = '`print("hi", 1)`'

 ansi_escape_run = re.compile(r"\x1b\[([0-9;]+)m([^\x1b]+)\x1b\[0m")


def render(renderable: RenderableType) -> str:
    console = Console(
        width=100, file=io.StringIO(), color_system="truecolor", legacy_windows=False
    )
    console.print(renderable)
    return console.file.getvalue()


def highlighted_runs(rendered: str) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """Get the (style, text) runs painted on the background of the code theme."""
    return [
        (style, text)
        for style, text in ansi_escape_run.findall(rendered)
        if "48;2" in style
    ]


def test_inline_code_in_table_body_cell():
    """Inline code in a body cell keeps the colors of the code theme."""
    markdown = Markdown(
        f"| Function |\n|---|\n| {SNIPPET} |\n", inline_code_lexer="python"
    )
    result = render(markdown)
    expected = '\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\x1b[36mFunction\x1b[0m\x1b[1m      \x1b[0m\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m ────────────── \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34mprint\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m(\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;230;219;116;48;2;39;40;34m"\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;230;219;116;48;2;39;40;34mhi\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;230;219;116;48;2;39;40;34m"\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m,\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m \x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;174;129;255;48;2;39;40;34m1\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m)\x1b[0m\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n'
    assert result == expected


def test_inline_code_in_table_heading_row():
    """Inline code in the heading row keeps the colors of the code theme too."""
    markdown = Markdown(
        f"| {SNIPPET} |\n|---|\n| done |\n", inline_code_lexer="python"
    )
    result = render(markdown)
    expected = '\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34mprint\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m(\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;230;219;116;48;2;39;40;34m"\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;230;219;116;48;2;39;40;34mhi\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;230;219;116;48;2;39;40;34m"\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m,\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m \x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;174;129;255;48;2;39;40;34m1\x1b[0m\x1b[38;2;248;248;242;48;2;39;40;34m)\x1b[0m\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m ────────────── \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0mdone          \x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n'
    assert result == expected


def test_inline_code_in_table_matches_paragraph():
    """A snippet in a cell looks the same as the same snippet in a sentence."""
    paragraph = render(
        Markdown(f"Text {SNIPPET} more", inline_code_lexer="python")
    )
    body_cell = render(
        Markdown(f"| Function |\n|---|\n| {SNIPPET} |\n", inline_code_lexer="python")
    )
    heading_cell = render(
        Markdown(f"| {SNIPPET} |\n|---|\n| done |\n", inline_code_lexer="python")
    )
    runs = highlighted_runs(paragraph)
    assert runs, "the snippet should be highlighted"
    assert highlighted_runs(body_cell) == runs
    assert highlighted_runs(heading_cell) == runs


def test_inline_code_in_table_without_lexer_is_unchanged():
    """Without a lexer, tables keep rendering exactly as they always did."""
    body_markdown = Markdown("| Function |\n|---|\n| " + SNIPPET + " |\n")
    body_result = render(body_markdown)
    body_expected = '\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\x1b[36mFunction\x1b[0m\x1b[1m      \x1b[0m\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m ────────────── \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\x1b[1;36;40mprint("hi", 1)\x1b[0m\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n'
    assert body_result == body_expected

    heading_markdown = Markdown("| " + SNIPPET + " |\n|---|\n| done |\n")
    heading_result = render(heading_markdown)
    heading_expected = '\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\x1b[36;40mprint("hi", 1)\x1b[0m\x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m ────────────── \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m \x1b[0mdone          \x1b[36m \x1b[0m\n\x1b[36m                \x1b[0m\n'
    assert heading_result == heading_expected


def test_plain_word_table_not_affected_by_lexer():
    """Tables of plain words look the same whether or not a lexer is given."""
    document = "| Function | Args |\n|---|---|\n| print | text |\n"
    without_lexer = render(Markdown(document))
    with_lexer = render(Markdown(document, inline_code_lexer="python"))
    assert with_lexer == without_lexer
    assert "48;2" not in without_lexer
